  • After the first objection, Delhi agents keep the meeting on the table more often: they ask for the meeting again in 17.5% of calls vs 11.9% in Mumbai, and name a time slot in 9.8% vs 6.1%.
  • The clearest difference is at the appointment ask. When the customer pushes back on the appointment, Mumbai agents give in 39.2% of the time vs 20.6% in Delhi.
  • Delhi agents use tactics that work in both cities more often. After “call me later”, they ask for the meeting again in 15% of calls vs 4% in Mumbai; after “busy now”, they ask when the customer is free in 19% vs 7%. When Mumbai agents do this, more than twice as many customers agree.
  • Projected uplift: if Mumbai agents used these tactics as often as Delhi agents, Mumbai would book about 1.2 more appointments (+6% on Mumbai's current bookings); matching Delhi's booked calls, about 2.1 more (+12%).

How objection handling differs

  • At the first objection, Delhi agents ask again more often (17.5% vs 11.9%) and less often close with a callback (21.7% vs 23.7%).
  • More Delhi customers agree: the customer agrees later in the call in 19.8% of Delhi calls with an objection vs 15.5% in Mumbai, and 4.0% of Delhi calls with an objection are booked vs 0.9%.
  • The gap is widest when the objection comes at the appointment ask (see “Handling by stage”).

Handling by stage: pitch, price and appointment push-back

  • “Gives in” = the agent ends with a callback, a WhatsApp promise or a goodbye, without asking for the meeting again.
  • Appointment push-back: the widest gap. Mumbai agents give in 39.2% of the time vs 20.6% in Delhi, and ask again in 16.3% vs 25.2%.
  • Price: Delhi slightly ahead. Agents give in 27.8% vs 22.6%, and ask again in 15.3% vs 20.2%.
  • Pitch: a small gap. Agents give in 27.0% vs 24.0%, and ask again in 14.9% vs 18.0%.
  • Bookings are appointments booked after an objection at that stage: Mumbai 1.4% (pitch), 2.1% (price), 1.3% (appointment ask); Delhi 6.0%, 4.8%, 6.5%.
  • Stage figures count every objection raised at that stage, not only the first one in the call, so they are not directly comparable with the first-objection figures above.

Tactics Delhi agents use to turn an objection round

  • Timing objections (“busy now”, “call me later”): Delhi agents ask when the customer is free, ask about the objection, or ask for the meeting again. These work in Mumbai too: when Mumbai agents use them, more than twice as many customers agree later in the call. After “busy now”, asking when the customer is free: 46% agree vs 16% without; asking for the meeting again: 35% vs 16%; asking about the objection: 28% vs 12%. After “call me later”, asking for the meeting again: 33% vs 10%.
  • Mumbai agents use them less often. After “call me later”, Mumbai agents ask for the meeting again in 4% of calls vs 15% in Delhi; after “busy now”, they ask when the customer is free in 7% vs 19%.

Projected appointment uplift for Mumbai

  • If Mumbai agents used these tactics as often as Delhi agents: about 19 more customers agree and 1.2 more appointments for Mumbai (+6% on current bookings).
  • If they matched Delhi agents in booked calls: about 35 more customers agree and 2.1 more appointments (+12%); 6.9 (+39%) if Mumbai also booked agreeing customers at Delhi's rate (20.0% vs 6.1%).
  • How the uplift is calculated:
    • Use rate: how often agents use a tactic after an objection. After “call me later”, Mumbai agents ask for the meeting again in 4% of calls vs 15% in Delhi, so the rise in use rate is 11 points.
    • Agree lift: how many more customers agree when the tactic is used. After “call me later”, 33% agree with it vs 10% without, a lift of 23 points.
    • Extra agreements = Mumbai calls with the objection × rise in use rate × agree lift.
    • Extra appointments = extra agreements × 6.1%, the share of agreeing Mumbai customers who get booked.

Example calls: the same objection, handled two ways

  • For each stage, the same objection in two calls: a Mumbai call where the agent gives in and the call is lost, next to a Delhi call where the agent turns the objection round and books the appointment.
  • Pitch: customer says “don't want it”. Price: customer wants to think it over and ask a partner. Appointment ask: customer is out or busy when the meeting is proposed.
  • Every call was read in full. In none of them had the customer agreed to a meeting before the objection. Delhi timings are exact; Mumbai timings are estimated from word counts, so key moments may be a few seconds off. Use “Play key moment only” to hear the exchange.

  • 200 randomly drawn calls (100 per city, matched on call length), each read and coded in full. 83 Delhi and 85 Mumbai calls were usable sales conversations with the business owner.
  • Each call coded on opening stance, response to price, response to the meeting ask, objections, how the call moves, closing stance and response style. Excluded: job seekers, consumers, closed businesses, non-owners, dead calls and likely hallucinated transcripts. About 13 of the 85 Mumbai calls are with merchants outside the Mumbai area. Engagement figures are medians from transcript text. Coded by one reader; treat small gaps as directional.
